messages:

Subject: Follow-up: today's discovery - perf targets & autoscaling

Thanks for the call today Marissa  helpful to get aligned on our performance needs. Quick recap from our side and a couple of clarifying questions: 

- Target p99 latency: <= 750ms for streaming chat (tokens streamed as available)
- Sustained throughput: ~5 requests/sec with average 6k prompt tokens, peaks to 20 req/sec for 30s bursts during shift changes
- Concurrency per conversational session: up to 8 parallel requests (multi-turn streaming)
- Requirement: no more than 2x SLO breach rate per week; we need graceful degradation (partial responses vs. hard failures)

Questions: 
1) How quickly can Redwood scale from idle to handle the 20 req/sec burst? 
2) Do warm pools / standby VMs keep KV cache warm for hot models? 
3) How does queueing behave if scale-up is in-progress  do you enqueue or fail fast?

If you can share a short note (and any attachments) that we can review with infra and procurement that would be great.

Alex
Director of Product
Acme Robotics

From: marissa_cole@redwood.com
To: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@acme-robotics.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@acme-robotics.com>, rishi_malhotra@redwood.com
Date: 2026-06-05T18:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: today's discovery - perf targets & autoscaling

Alex  thanks for the clear summary. Good questions; below is a short answers + proposed next steps. I'm attaching our SLO template and an initial capacity estimate for the burst profile.

Answers (short):
- Scale-up time: typical cold-to-warm scale for a new shard is ~6090s (GPU provisioning + model load) on Hosted. For Dedicated reserved pools with warm standby nodes, we see 820s for routing to an already-warmed instance.
- Warm pools: yes  Dedicated and Private options support warm pools with KV/LLM cache priming. For Hosted we do a hot-spotting option (keep N instances warm for high-priority customers).
- Queueing behavior: by default requests are queued (short FIFO buffer ~10s) while we spin up capacity; beyond that we surface a 429 with Retry-After. We can configure aggressive queuing + soft-degradation (stream partial tokens) for your use case.

Notes on SLO fit:
- Streaming p99 <= 750ms: achievable with a warm pool and continuous batching disabled for low latency. We recommend a mix of 2 warm nodes + autoscale to reach peak.
- Peak 20 req/sec (6k tokens avg): with our standard A100-like pool, rough estimate in attachment suggests 2 warmed GPUs + scale to 6 GPUs for sustained peaks (see capacity-estimate-acme.xlsx).
- Concurrency: per-session concurrency of 8 is fine; we recommend connection multiplexing and token-based concurrency limits to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Next steps:
1) I'll sync with Rishi (copying) to produce a recommended warm-pool config + cost tradeoffs.
2) If helpful, we can schedule a short technical call with infra (30 min) to walk scaling behavior and logs.
3) I'll include an SLO doc you can share with procurement.

Attaching: redwood-slo-template.pdf, capacity-estimate-acme.xlsx

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Sales Engineer
Redwood Inference

Alex / Marissa  adding a few technical details to Marissa's notes that Alex's infra team will want to check: 

- Warm-pool semantics: "warmed" nodes have model weights and tokenizer loaded; KV cache priming is per-customer and improves p99 for repeated prefixes but is not globally shared. We can pre-warm KV cache by running synthetic prefixes at low cost during off hours.
- Scale path: requests -> ingress routing -> routing policy (latency-first) -> if local capacity insufficient we attempt remote region/fallback model variant (quantized) before queuing.
- Queueing: we expose two knobs: max-queue-ms (how long we hold requests) and max-queue-depth. We recommend max-queue-ms=10000ms and soft-fail (stream partial) for Acme to avoid hard failures during 30s bursts.
- Observability: we emit token-level latency histograms and queue_depth_{p50,p95,p99} metrics to the customer console/Prometheus. We can instrument a short experiment to validate warm pool sizing (1h soak during a simulated shift-change).

I captured a sample warm-pool config in-line: 
- warm_pool_size: 2 nodes (model: open-llama-13B-quant)
- scale_up_step: +2 nodes every 15s until max (6)
- pre_warm_kv: true (run 5k synthetic prefixes per node)
- queueing: enabled, max_queue_ms: 10000

I'll follow up with a one-pager and cost estimate.

-rishi
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference

Thanks  this is great context. A couple clarifying items from procurement/infra: 

- For the warm pool option on Dedicated, what SLA/uptime guarantee can we get for the warmed capacity? We need to understand financial/contractary implications.
- Can you confirm whether the warm nodes are billed while idle (we expect yes) and if so, what the monthly delta looks like for the recommended 2-node warm pool?
- On queueing: we prefer soft-degrade (partial tokens) vs. 429s for user experience; does Redwood support a fallback to a smaller quantized model automatically if scaling misses the window?

If you can provide a short answer to these three items we'll include in the procurement packet.

Priya
Head of Infrastructure
Acme Robotics

From: marissa_cole@redwood.com

Priya  answers below so you can drop into your packet. Looping Dev (acct exec) for PO/contract questions.

1) SLA for warm capacity: For Dedicated customers we can add a warmed-node SLA as an add-on (99.9% for reserved warm pool availability). This is typically added to the Dedicated contract as a capacity reservation with credits for missed availability.

2) Billing for warm nodes: yes warmed nodes are billed while idle as reserved capacity. Rough delta: two warm A100-like nodes estimate ~$12k/month (region dependent). Exact numbers in the capacity-estimate-acme.xlsx. We can present an annual commit vs. month-to-month comparison.

3) Fallback to quantized model: yes  routing policy supports automatic fallback to a compatible quantized/variant model when primary capacity is constrained. The fallback behavior is configurable: (a) prefer quantized with same output format; (b) stream partial tokens and tag with provenance header; or (c) fail fast. We suggest option (a) + stream partial tokens for best user experience.

Next steps: 
- Dev will follow up on contract language and PO workflow.
- Rishi and I will schedule a 30-min runbook session to confirm config and a 1h soak test.
- If Acme is comfortable, we can provision a 2-week pilot on a warm Dedicated pool to validate SLOs.

Happy to jump on a call to walk your procurement team through the SLA language.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Sales Engineer
Redwood Inference
